PMGT1711 Week 02

PMGT1711 Week 02 - Project Complexity, Mental Models and Learning Loops

Overview

Projects are shaped by how people understand them, and by how those understandings change. This week covers:

• Mental models: the internal frameworks that explain how the world works, and the assumptions hidden inside them.

• Learning loops: single-loop, double-loop and triple-loop learning, and the question each one asks.

• The Ladder of Inference, a framework for how people move from observable data to action, and how to make that reasoning explicit.

• Hard Systems Thinking (HST) and Soft Systems Thinking (SST): two families of systems approaches with different assumptions about goals, knowledge and inquiry.

• A methods-positioning grid that relates system complexity and stakeholder relations.

• Eleven laws of systems behaviour that explain why well-meant interventions in complex systems so often backfire.

Key Concepts

Mental models

Mental models are the internal concepts, frameworks and worldviews a person uses to explain how things work. They filter what people notice and how they interpret it. Because they operate silently, they must be surfaced (made explicit) and tested against evidence rather than assumed to be correct. Assumptions - the taken-for-granted claims inside a mental model - are the specific points that need checking.

Hard Systems Thinking (HST)

Hard Systems Thinking approaches start from a known current state (call it S0) and a desired future state (call it S1) that is defined clearly enough to work towards. The task is then to compare alternative routes to S1 against performance measures and choose the best one.

• The HST methodology is explicitly iterative, not a one-shot waterfall: define the problem, analyse the situation, set objectives and constraints, identify routes and performance measures, develop, evaluate and select options, implement, then revisit and iterate.

• Named hard methods include:

◦ Systems analysis (SA): examines facts, goals, components, alternatives and their consequences.

◦ Systems engineering (SE): integrates disciplines and requirements across development and the life cycle.

◦ Operational research (OR): uses scientific modelling and analysis to support decisions.

◦ System dynamics (SD): models stocks, flows and feedback in a system over time (quantitative simulation and control-oriented use).

• These method definitions overlap but are not mutually exclusive and not interchangeable.

• Example of a structured hard method: Six Sigma's DMAIC cycle - Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control.

Soft Systems Thinking (SST)

Soft Systems Thinking approaches start from a problematic situation in which the desired end state (call it Sx) is itself contested. There are several competing formulations of the situation (S1 to Sn), none of them complete, and different worldviews judge the same actions differently. The goal is not to optimise towards a fixed target but to learn about the situation and find improvements that are both desirable and feasible.

• SST emphasises qualitative participation - dialogue, questionnaires, focus groups - and learning through the inquiry itself.

• Named soft methods include SSM (Soft Systems Methodology), CSH (Critical Systems Heuristics) and Interactive Planning.

• SSM produces models of learning, not guaranteed consensus: it does not deliver the one correct picture of a social system, and agreement among stakeholders is not assured.

Hard and soft approaches differ mainly in their assumptions about goals, perspectives and the mode of inquiry - not simply in whether they use numbers or words. A hard study can be iterative and holistic, and a soft study can use quantitative evidence.

Learning loops: single, double and triple

Learning can operate at three depths:

Loop

What is changed

The question it asks

Single-loop

Actions, routines and practices are adjusted while existing assumptions stay fixed; feedback corrects what you do

Are we doing things right?

Double-loop

The causal understanding, assumptions and policies behind the actions are revised

Are we doing the right things?

Triple-loop

The frameworks, values and criteria by which learning and governance are judged are revised - how the organisation decides what counts as right

How do we decide what is right?

Frameworks and Formulas

Ladder of Inference

The Ladder of Inference describes the rungs people climb, usually in an instant, between observable reality and the actions they take:

Observable reality and available data: everything that could in principle be observed.

Selected data: the subset of reality the person actually notices.

Meanings: the interpretation attached to the selected data.

Assumptions: the beliefs taken for granted while interpreting.

Conclusions: what the person decides is true.

Beliefs: the mental model that results and is stored for later.

Actions: what the person does based on the belief.

The reflexive loop is the feedback from beliefs back to step 2: once a belief is formed, it influences which data the person selects next time, which can reinforce confirmation bias (seeking and noticing only evidence that fits existing beliefs).

Working with the ladder:

• Ask yourself: What did I actually observe, and what did I infer? What am I missing? Why did I make this assumption? What other explanations also fit the evidence?

• In dialogue: state the evidence you selected and your reasoning, restate the other person's interpretation to check you understood it, and invite them to add evidence you missed or propose alternative interpretations.

Methods-positioning grid

Systems methods can be positioned on two dimensions: system complexity (how complex the situation is) and stakeholder relations (how the people involved relate to one another).

Stakeholder relations

Meaning

Unitary

Shared values; stakeholders are broadly aligned in interest

Pluralist

Different values, but sufficiently common interests to negotiate

Coercive

Values and interests in conflict; power decides

Hard systems approaches are typically positioned in the simple-to-complicated, unitary region of this grid. This is a positioning heuristic only: it does not mean hard methods are incapable of complicated engineering problems, nor that soft methods never use numbers.

Eleven laws of systems behaviour

These laws describe recurring patterns in complex systems (presented here as teaching heuristics, not as strict universal laws):

Today's problems come from yesterday's solutions: quick fixes and burden-shifting create tomorrow's difficulties.

The harder you push, the more the system pushes back through compensating feedback.

Because of delays, short-term improvements can be followed by deterioration.

The easy way out often leads back to where you started.

The cure can be worse than the disease, and can create dependence on further intervention.

Faster can be slower: work that is skipped becomes rework later.

Causes and effects are separated in both time and space.

Small, high-leverage changes can produce large effects that are not immediately obvious.

Apparent trade-offs can change over time.

Half an elephant is not two elephants: dividing a system destroys the wholeness of its relationships.

There is no separate "them" to blame: examine the system's conditions and your own part in it.

Worked Examples

A two-month delay: climbing the ladder wrongly

A project ran two months late. The manager noticed that three design approvals were still pending, but overlooked a delay in a council permit that the approvals depended on. From the selected data (pending design approvals) the manager inferred poor design performance and added supervision and resources to the design work. The error occurred at the selected data rung: the data set was incomplete, so every rung above it - meaning, assumption, conclusion, action - rested on a partial picture. The correct response is to check the underlying dependencies (here, the permit) before accepting the diagnosis as proven.

Segura River: hard methods still integrate people

A study of the Segura River involved sewage infrastructure, the operating agencies, monitoring, regulation and taxation, and public consultation together. The example shows that using hard approaches does not mean ignoring system integration or the people in the system: physical infrastructure, organisations, regulation and the public are all parts of the system being analysed.

Mental models in health care: deciding what kind of learning occurred

A class exercise on mental models and high blood pressure: participants write down their beliefs about whether high blood pressure should be treated and whether medication, reduced salt, exercise, sleep, stress reduction and diet help; link each belief to an action they would take; and draft a care plan for a patient. They then read a current medical article and ask whether their model or plan changed, and if so, classify the change: adjusting the plan is single-loop, revising the causal beliefs about what helps is double-loop, and changing the rules by which they select and evaluate medical information (for example, broadening and scrutinising their usual sources) is triple-loop. Two lessons follow. First, merely consulting one extra source is not automatically triple-loop: what matters is what changed - an action, a causal model, or the rules for choosing and judging knowledge. Second, the reliability of any source still has to be assessed; the exercise concerns learning and assumptions and is not a basis for medical treatment decisions.
